passage: At the holiday sports camp, Yogesh, five, held Dhruv's sleeve. "You're my best friend. Only you." A girl named Tina came over with a ball. "No, she can't play," said Yogesh. Dhruv looked at the ball, then at Yogesh. The coach knelt. "Being best friends is lovely. Is there room for Tina too, without anyone feeling pushed out?" Yogesh chewed his lip. "She can be goalie." Dhruv smiled at Tina.

qa.q: Who did Yogesh say could not play?
qa.a: Tina, the girl who came over with a ball.

qa.q: What might Yogesh be worried about when he shut Tina out?
qa.a: Possibly losing Dhruv's closeness, or being left out himself. He might also simply want the game to stay as it was.

qa.q: How did the coach teach loyalty without hurting anyone?
qa.a: The coach praised the friendship and asked whether there was room for Tina too, so closeness could include others.

qa.q: How might Tina feel when told she cannot play?
qa.a: Probably hurt or left out, until Yogesh offered her the goalie spot.

grounding: Shows a preschooler declaring a best friend and excluding another child, with a coach teaching that closeness can include others.

passage: I'm Maria, and I watch the sandpit from the bench. Simran, five, told my daughter, "You're my best friend." Then she turned to a third child. "Go away, she's mine." The third child's face fell. My daughter said, "We can all dig." Simran hesitated. "Okay, but I dig next to her." I can't tell whether Simran was scared of losing her friend or just very excited.

qa.q: What did Simran tell Maria's daughter?
qa.a: "You're my best friend."

qa.q: Why might Simran have said "Go away, she's mine"?
qa.a: Possibly fear of losing her friend to someone else, or excitement about having her all to herself.

qa.q: How could an adult help Simran keep her closeness without shutting others out?
qa.a: Tell her she can keep her best friend and still share the sandpit, and suggest a way for all three to dig.

qa.q: How did the third child likely feel?
qa.a: Hurt and left out, shown by the third child's face falling.

grounding: Shows a child saying you are my best friend and excluding a third child, seen by a parent on a bench.

passage:
Monday: At the colony sandpit, Chinmay told Kiaan, “Arun is my best friend. You can't play with us.” Kiaan walked away slowly. Vishal, Chinmay's father, saw it.
Tuesday: At bedtime Vishal said, “You love Arun, and that's lovely. But how did Kiaan feel yesterday?” Chinmay thought. “Sad.” “Can best friends still play with other kids?” “…Maybe.”
Thursday: Chinmay called, “Kiaan! You can be the digger driver. Arun and me are the builders.” The three of them dug a tunnel together.

qa.q: What job did Chinmay give Kiaan on Thursday?
qa.a: Digger driver.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay tell Kiaan he couldn't play?
qa.a: He felt fond and loyal to Arun and wanted to keep him close, not realising it would hurt Kiaan.

qa.q: What did Vishal do that helped Chinmay include Kiaan?
qa.a: He praised Chinmay's love for Arun, then asked how Kiaan felt and whether best friends can play with others, so Chinmay found the answer himself.

qa.q: What was it like for Kiaan when he was told he couldn't play?
qa.a: He was hurt and left out, which is why he walked away slowly.

grounding: Over a week, a child learns that loyalty to a best friend doesn't mean excluding and hurting another child.

passage: Rain kept the whole class indoors, and there was only one small play kitchen. Vasudha stood in front of it with her friend Tia, arms out. “Only me and Tia. We're best friends.” A new girl, holding a toy pot, stepped back. Samir Sir came over. “You two love playing together. That's nice. Can best friends make room for a cook?” Vasudha frowned. “But then it's not just us.” “It can still be you two, plus one.” Tia whispered, “She can be the guest.” Vasudha shrugged. “Okay. Guest.”

qa.q: What was the new girl holding?
qa.a: A toy pot.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she frowned at Samir Sir's idea?
qa.a: She felt worried that letting someone in would spoil her closeness with Tia.

qa.q: How did Samir Sir help Vasudha see closeness differently?
qa.a: He praised the friendship and suggested it could still be the two of them plus one, so closeness could include others.

qa.q: How might the new girl feel when she's invited as the guest?
qa.a: She'd likely feel relieved and included after being shut out.

grounding: On a crowded indoor day, a child tries to keep her best friend to herself, and her teacher shows closeness can include others.

passage: In the colony lane, Asif hooked his arm round Ramesh's neck. “You're my best friend, so don't play with Kunal. Promise?” Ramesh looked at Kunal, who was holding a cricket bat and waiting. He didn't know what to say. Asif's Ammi, drying clothes on the balcony, called down. “Asif, being best friends is good. But telling Ramesh not to play with Kunal hurts Kunal. You can be best friends and still play together.” Asif pouted, then let go. “Okay. Kunal bats first.”

qa.q: What was Kunal holding?
qa.a: A cricket bat.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when Asif asked him to promise?
qa.a: He was probably torn and uncomfortable, caught between his best friend and Kunal, who was waiting to play.

qa.q: What did Asif's Ammi teach about loyalty?
qa.a: That being best friends is good, but it shouldn't mean hurting someone else, and all three could play.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Asif's words?
qa.a: Kunal would feel left out and hurt, since he was being kept away on purpose.

grounding: A child tries to keep his best friend away from another boy, and his mother teaches that loyalty does not mean hurting someone else.

passage:
"Pallavi, you're my best friend. So you can't play with the new girl."

Pallavi looked at the new girl, standing alone by the sandpit. "But she's got a bucket."

"Best friends only play with each other," Yamini insisted, grabbing Pallavi's arm.

Their teacher crouched beside them. "Yamini, you and Pallavi are very close. That's lovely. Can best friends play with someone else too?"

Yamini frowned. "Then Pallavi won't like me as much."

"Does your Amma love you less when she talks to your Nani?"

"...No."

"Shall we ask the new girl to build a castle with you both?"

Yamini sighed. "Okay. But I'm doing the tower."

qa.q: Where was the new girl standing?
qa.a: Alone by the sandpit.

qa.q: Why did Yamini want Pallavi to play only with her?
qa.a: She was most likely worried that sharing Pallavi would mean being liked less; she said so herself. Grabbing Pallavi's arm shows how strongly she wanted to hold on to her friend.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Yamini see that closeness can include others?
qa.a: The teacher praised their friendship, then used an everyday example about Amma and Nani, and suggested building a castle together.

qa.q: How might the new girl feel while Yamini keeps Pallavi to herself?
qa.a: She is probably lonely and left out, standing alone with her bucket, hoping someone will let her join.

grounding: It shows a young child calling someone her best friend and excluding another child, and an adult teaching that closeness can include others.
